1:
The title is the first difficulty. Delitzsch pairs the psalm with the one before it, where the poet likewise called himself a dumb man who opens not his mouth, and more closely with a later psalm of the same background, both carrying Jeduthun's name beside David's. Clarke reports the guess that Jeduthun is Ethan, one of the four masters of music at the temple, to whose company David gave the psalm to sing — though several have supposed Jeduthun wrote it. Calvin thinks the singer's household the likely explanation and refuses two alternatives: that the name marks a tune, which he calls too forced, and that David complains of a particular disease, since it is improper to narrow a general statement without urgent reason. From the extremity of the suffering he judges a variety of afflictions is meant, or one severer than the rest that had lasted long.

Augustine takes the name for the psalm's subject, not its singer. Jeduthun translated is one over-leaping them — and those over-leaped are the people still clinging to the earth, bowed to the ground, setting their hearts on what is below and their hopes on what passes away. He connects this with the psalms of degrees, whose Greek title means steps of those ascending.

On the resolution itself they are agreed and thorough. Henry reads the verse as David reminding himself of covenants already made: when we are tempted and near falling we must call to mind the solemn vows we made against that very sin, since God himself will remind us of them. He puts the general resolution first — it is every man's great concern to take heed to his ways, and to renew that resolve often, for fast bind, fast find — and then the particular one against tongue-sins. It is not easy to avoid sinning in thought, but if an evil thought arises David would lay his hand on his mouth and suppress it; the bridle is kept on his mouth as on a head, the muzzle as on an unruly dog. Spurgeon says the same in his own key. It is excellent when a man strengthens himself in a good course by remembering a well-formed resolve; unguarded ways are generally unholy, and heedless is another word for graceless. He adds why tongue-sins matter here: if believers utter hard words of God in depression, the ungodly take them up as justification for their own courses; and if a man's own children rail at him, no wonder his enemies' mouths are full of abuse.

Ellicott supplies what the others assume, which is how unnatural the silence was. To feel the verse one must remember the unrestrained way Orientals give way to grief: it was natural for this poet to roar out his indignation, to mutter his prayers aloud, to speak on every impulse. What he now determines is to endure in silence and mutely bear the worst, rather than say anything the impious could construe as a murmur against providence. On the bridle Ellicott gives the root-meaning as stop, and gathers the parallels — the epistle of James, Virgil, and Plato's remark that an argument, like a horse, ought to be pulled up from time to time and not allowed to run away, but held with bit and bridle.

Clarke reads the silence practically and gives three reasons at once: he must be cautious because of his enemies, patient because of his afflictions, and watchful over his tongue lest he offend God or give his adversaries cause to speak evil of him. He also fixes the occasion, taking the psalm with the one before and referring it to the malady that followed the affair with Bathsheba. Wesley reduces the verse to two clauses — I fully resolved; to order all my actions right, and particularly to govern my tongue — and Gill notes that David put the resolution into practice.
2:
The silence does not work, and everyone says so. Gill notes David was quite silent, as though dumb; Wesley that two words are put together to aggravate the thing, the silence not assuaging the grief but increasing it. Clarke states the general case as a balance: it is hard to be denied the benefit of complaint, which relieves the mind and calls attention off the place of suffering, and yet extravagant complaint enervates the mind so that it becomes a double prey to its own sufferings. There are extremes on both sides, and he thinks David steered clear of them on the right hand and the left.

Ellicott disputes the rendering of verse 2. The clause held my peace even from good follows the Greek, the Latin and most ancient versions, but is suspicious: the particle rendered from is not generally used in that sense after a verb of silence, and only one passage supports it. Nor does the context want it, since if the bright side had been evident enough to speak of, the psalmist would not have feared reproach — and the rabbinical explanation, that he was silent as to the law, is no better. The obvious translation makes the clause parallel to what follows: I held my peace without profit, and my sorrow was increased.

What it does instead is told three ways. Clarke takes the heat for a natural feeling of repressed grief, and the musing for a metaphor from vegetables heaped together, which ferment if not scattered and soon produce a flame consuming themselves and everything within reach. Ellicott has repression making the inward flame burn more fiercely till it is too much for the resolution and the passion of the heart breaks into words — not fretfully, he adds, still less in bitter invective against others, but as a dialogue with the ruler of destiny in which frail man wants to face his condition and know the worst. Spurgeon's version is the most physical: the door of the heart was shut with the fire of sorrow burning inside, and silence is an awful thing for a sufferer, the surest way to produce madness. While the heart was musing it was fusing, for the subject was confusing; an eruption was imminent. Mourner, he says, tell your sorrow — first and most fully to God, but pouring it out before a wise and godly friend is far from wasted breath.

What breaks out is a request for the date of his death. Gill thinks it said in a passionate way, as one impatient of his exercises, and reads it as a request for death itself, not for information. Ellicott marks the verse as the point from which all is the utterance the poet's feelings have driven him to, and prefers frail to the marginal reading, the Hebrew root meaning to leave off and here implying ceasing to live. Delitzsch gives the request its logic: if life is only a few spans long, the suffering and the prosperity of the ungodly will both last a short time, so what is asked is that God set the transitoriness of life plainly before his eyes. Wesley glosses it as being made sensible of the shortness of life and the near approach of death.

The answer is measurement. Gill treats the handbreadth as a correction of the impatient question, since it was needless to ask when life was so short: not a yard or an ell, nor even a span, but the breadth of four fingers. Clarke observes that before God all time is swallowed up in eternity. Ellicott gathers the poets, man as a shadow being a commonplace from Pindar down through Sophocles, Horace and Burke, and sets Shakespeare beside both halves — a breath thou art, and life's but a walking shadow, a poor player. Wesley makes it shorter: before thee means if compared with thy everlasting duration.
7:
Verse 7 concludes from all before it, and Henry states the logic: seeing all is vanity and man himself is so, the psalmist disclaims all expectation from the world, life's frailty deadening our desires toward it. Then he takes hold of the other thing: when creature-confidences fail it is our comfort that we have a God to go to, and should lay faster hold on him. Spurgeon reads the movement as disgust rather than despair: the psalmist has thought on the world and all in it, is relieved that such things are passing, and cuts the cords binding him to earth. Ellicott insists on what is not there: the poet can turn to no hope of immortality, since that had not yet dawned; what raises him above the oppressive sense of frailty is God's mercy and the hope of his own moral deliverance.

Verse 8 asks pardon before relief, and Henry marks the order: David prays to be delivered from his offences — the guilt contracted, the punishment deserved, the corruption that enslaved him — before asking that the stroke be removed. The plea that follows he reads as a prayer both for peace of conscience and for grace: that the writer not be left to a melancholy the foolish would laugh at, nor to himself so far as to earn their scorn. Ellicott finds the same in the structure: the fear that the wicked might find cause for reproach was no fancy, since the cause was already there in the poet's consciousness of transgression. Clarke wants the deliverance to be evidence, so the godless who deride him may learn there is a God who hears prayer.

Then the silence returns, and Gill notes the difference: the dumbness of verse 9 is not that of verse 2, which was impatience held in, but a man who has seen the vanity of things and put his hope in God. Henry gives the reason as the psalm gives it — because thou didst it. Of every event we may say this is the finger of God, whoever were the instruments; and a good man has then nothing to object. Ellicott quotes Kimchi more tightly: I could not complain of man, for it was God's doing; nor of God, for I was conscious of my own sin.

The last petitions are physical. Clarke hears in remove thy stroke a figure from single combat: a fighter wounded past continuing gives in and prays his adversary to spare him, crying what our ancestors called craven. Wesley reads it as asking that the judgment be taken off before he is lost; Gill is careful that such asking does not contradict the silence just professed. Henry adds the condition on which it may be asked in faith: when our sins are pardoned and the affliction has done its work. Delitzsch notes the prayer is renewed here, based on the shortness of the pilgrimage.

Verse 11 says why none can hold out. Clarke reads rebukes as a legal term: when God maintains his law's authority the culprit's beauty consumes away, as a man whose guilt is proved grows pale and faints in court. Henry divides it: we cannot impeach the equity of the controversy, correction being always for iniquity and the rod of our own making, nor escape it. Ellicott makes the image exact — thou, like a moth consuming a garment, causest his desirable things to melt — apt where raiment was hoarded as wealth. Wesley takes the moth for God's judgments, secretly consuming a people. On the closing plea Ellicott hears Abraham's words about being a stranger applied to the earthly pilgrimage, and asks the psalm's own question: why, when life's tenure is so uncertain, does God look angrily on him? Clarke answers that the psalmist never made this earth his home; Gill reads the last cry as asking God to turn away his fierce countenance.
